set.explanation: A young woman with a preceding systemic illness (fever, myalgia), exertional chest pain, breathlessness and an absent radial pulse on one side has Takayasu arteritis, a granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta and its branches ('pulseless disease'). It is diagnosed by CT or MR angiography showing wall thickening and stenoses and treated with corticosteroids. Type B dissection causes severe tearing pain, myocarditis does not abolish pulses, and an embolus would cause acute limb ischaemia.

Progressive breathlessness, orthopnoea, pink frothy sputum, bibasal crackles, a raised JVP, oedema and cardiomegaly in a man with hypertension and coronary disease is acute decompensated (congestive) heart failure with pulmonary oedema. COPD and asthma cause wheeze without a raised JVP or cardiomegaly, pulmonary embolism is sudden with clear lungs, and ARDS follows a precipitating insult with a normal-sized heart.

The immediate treatment of congestion in acute heart failure is an IV loop diuretic such as furosemide, together with oxygen if hypoxic, sitting up, and IV nitrates if the BP allows. An ARB is not started acutely (and he already takes an ACE inhibitor), diltiazem is negatively inotropic, and heparin and clopidogrel treat thrombosis rather than congestion.

Complications of heart failure and its treatment include atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, hyponatraemia (from neurohormonal activation and diuretics), hyperkalaemia (from ACE inhibitors, MRAs and renal impairment) and a raised urea from reduced renal perfusion (cardiorenal syndrome). Hyperlipidaemia is a risk factor for the underlying coronary disease, not a consequence of heart failure.

Transthoracic echocardiography is the key investigation in suspected heart failure: it measures ejection fraction (classifying HFrEF, HFmrEF or HFpEF) and shows valve disease, regional wall-motion abnormalities, pericardial disease and filling pressures. The ECG, blood gases and electrolytes support management, and coronary angiography comes later if ischaemia is suspected as the cause.

Spironolactone, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, improves symptoms and mortality in HFrEF (RALES) and adds a mild diuretic effect. Non-selective propranolol is not an evidence-based heart-failure beta-blocker (he already takes bisoprolol), flecainide increases mortality in structural heart disease, NSAIDs such as meloxicam cause fluid retention and worsen heart failure, and bretylium is an obsolete antiarrhythmic.

topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
set.explanation: When ACE inhibitors, ARBs or ARNI cannot be used because of renal impairment or hyperkalaemia, hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate reduces mortality in HFrEF (V-HeFT, A-HeFT) and does not raise potassium. Sacubitril/valsartan and spironolactone are contraindicated with a potassium of 5.4 mmol/L and an eGFR of 25, ivabradine needs sinus rhythm at 70/min or more despite beta-blockade and only reduces hospitalisation, and digoxin does not improve survival.

topics: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
set.explanation: In HFpEF, SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin in DELIVER, empagliflozin in EMPEROR-Preserved) reduce heart-failure hospitalisation and cardiovascular death, regardless of diabetes, and are now recommended first-line alongside diuretics for congestion and treatment of comorbidities (BP, OSA, obesity). Spironolactone and sacubitril/valsartan have weaker, borderline evidence, and nitrates and beta-blockers have no outcome benefit in HFpEF.

New LV systolic dysfunction late in pregnancy is peripartum cardiomyopathy. During pregnancy it is treated with a beta-blocker (metoprolol) and a loop diuretic for congestion, with hydralazine and nitrates for afterload reduction if needed. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, ARNI and MRAs are teratogenic or unsafe before delivery, and ivabradine is not used. Anticoagulation is advised when the EF is very low, and bromocriptine may be considered after delivery.

ACE inhibitors (or ARB/ARNI), evidence-based beta-blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate), MRAs and SGLT2 inhibitors all reduce mortality in HFrEF. Digoxin reduced hospitalisation but not mortality in the DIG trial; it is used for rate control in AF or for persistent symptoms despite optimal therapy.

why: Same idea as hf-0009 (digoxin does not improve survival in heart failure)

set.explanation: In an older adult with a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle, coronary disease must be excluded (by CT coronary angiography, invasive angiography or MRI) before labelling it non-ischaemic, because revascularisation may help. Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy cause dilated systolic dysfunction, HCM is the leading cause of sudden death in young athletes, restrictive cardiomyopathy is the hardest to diagnose (it mimics constriction), and CRT is used in HFrEF with a broad QRS, not HCM.

A patient with heart failure who takes only a loop diuretic and aspirin is missing prognostic therapy; an ACE inhibitor (enalapril) should be started and titrated, which also treats her hypertension, followed by a beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor. Thiazides only add diuresis, nitrates do not improve prognosis on their own, and spironolactone is added once ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker are established.

A young woman with biventricular failure (raised JVP, tender hepatomegaly, oedema, crackles, S3), cardiomegaly and global LV hypokinesia with an EF of 25–30% has dilated cardiomyopathy with congestive failure. Restrictive cardiomyopathy and constriction have preserved systolic function, HCM shows a thick non-dilated ventricle, and valvular disease would produce a significant murmur and echo findings.

set.stem: A 30-year-old woman has dilated cardiomyopathy with biventricular failure and an ejection fraction of 25–30%. Which of the following is a cornerstone of the medical treatment of her systolic heart failure?
topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
set.explanation: ACE inhibitors reduce mortality and hospitalisation in HFrEF by reducing afterload and adverse remodelling; they are a cornerstone of therapy (or ARB, or sacubitril/valsartan in place of either), together with beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2 inhibitors. Non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers worsen HFrEF, most antiarrhythmics are harmful, and nitrates alone do not improve survival.

set.stem: In the same woman with dilated cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 25–30%, which of the following is another key medication?
topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
set.explanation: Beta-blockers proven in HFrEF (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, nebivolol) reduce mortality by about a third and improve ejection fraction. They are started at a low dose once the patient is euvolaemic and titrated slowly. Statins and anticoagulants have no general role in non-ischaemic DCM unless there is another indication, and steroids are only for specific inflammatory causes.

set.stem: In the same woman with dilated cardiomyopathy, oedema and pulmonary crackles, which of the following is also an important part of her medical therapy?
set.explanation: Loop diuretics relieve congestion (oedema, crackles, raised JVP) and symptoms in heart failure, but do not improve survival, so the dose is kept to the minimum needed for euvolaemia. Antiplatelet agents are for coronary disease, antibiotics only for infection, and calcium-channel blockers (apart from amlodipine for hypertension or angina) should be avoided in HFrEF.

set.stem: Which complication is commonly associated with dilated cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction?
set.explanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy predisposes to atrial fibrillation and ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden arrhythmic death is a major cause of mortality; an ICD is considered when the EF stays at 35% or less despite optimal therapy. Pulmonary fibrosis, aortic dissection and pericardial effusion are not typical complications.

set.stem: Which of the following is another potential complication of dilated cardiomyopathy?
set.explanation: Stasis of blood in a dilated, poorly contracting ventricle (and in the atria if AF develops) predisposes to mural thrombus and systemic embolism such as stroke; anticoagulation is indicated for AF or a documented LV thrombus. Varices and cirrhosis would need long-standing congestive hepatopathy, and COPD and MI are not complications of DCM.

set.stem: In a patient with dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure, an audible third heart sound most likely indicates:
set.explanation: An S3 in early diastole reflects rapid ventricular filling into a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle with high filling pressures; in adults over 40 it is a sign of heart failure (a gallop rhythm). An opening snap indicates mitral stenosis, a pericardial knock indicates constriction, and RV hypertrophy gives a right-sided S4. ASD produces fixed splitting of S2.

Causes of dilated cardiomyopathy include alcohol, iron overload (haemochromatosis), myocarditis, genetic mutations, pregnancy, drugs (anthracyclines) and persistent tachycardia; Wilson's disease is a rarer cause. Hypertension typically causes concentric LV hypertrophy and diastolic (HFpEF) dysfunction; it can end in a dilated ventricle, but it is the least likely cause of DCM among these.

Mutations in beta-myosin heavy chain (MYH7) are classically associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, although some MYH7 variants can cause DCM. Alcohol, pregnancy (peripartum cardiomyopathy) and long-standing tachycardia (tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy) are established causes of DCM, and the last two may reverse if the cause is removed.

In a breathless patient with both COPD and ischaemic heart disease, a gallop rhythm (S3) is the most specific sign that the crackles come from left ventricular failure with raised filling pressure. Tachycardia is non-specific, pulsus alternans is rare and indicates severe LV dysfunction, and peripheral oedema with a normal JVP points away from right-sided or biventricular failure.

why: Same question as hf-0009 (digoxin does not improve prognosis in heart failure)
Same idea as hf-0001 (pink frothy sputum with gallop rhythm = pulmonary oedema of heart failure)

topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
set.explanation: Heart failure is classified by LVEF: reduced (HFrEF) at 40% or less, mildly reduced (HFmrEF) at 41–49%, and preserved (HFpEF) at 50% or more with evidence of raised filling pressures. High-output failure (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, AV fistula) is a separate physiological category, and 'right-sided' describes the side affected rather than the EF.

The ACC/AHA stages are: A, at risk (for example hypertension or diabetes) without structural disease; B, structural heart disease without symptoms; C, structural disease with current or previous symptoms; and D, refractory heart failure needing advanced therapies. The NYHA classes I–IV grade symptoms separately. There is no stage E.

why: Same idea as hf-0014 (ACE inhibitors are a cornerstone of HFrEF therapy)
Same idea as hf-0004 (echocardiography is the key investigation in heart failure)

set.explanation: In HFrEF (EF 35% or less) with LBBB and a QRS of 150 ms or more despite optimal medical therapy, biventricular pacing (CRT) restores synchronous contraction, improves EF and symptoms, and reduces mortality; a CRT-D adds a defibrillator. Extra diuretic only treats congestion, angioplasty only helps ischaemia, and an ICD alone prevents sudden death without improving LV function.
